title: Reimagining the relationship between data centers & the Canadian power grid
transcriptText:
Hi everyone, and thanks for joining me
and Cliff here today. My name is Matt,
head of conference production over at
Data Center Nation. For those who of you
who may have not heard of us before, we
organize industry-leading conferences
and expos in emerging data center
markets across North America and the
EMEA region with the mission of
providing national data center
ecosystems with a unique platform to
network with their peers and share
ideas.
Our sister company is, of course, Data
Center Dynamics, where I was also there
for 2 years previously, leading the
North American portfolio of events. So,
it's great to be joined with Cliff here
today to chat about our upcoming
Canadian events.
Well, thank you, Matt, and
as Matt said, I'm Cliff Grosner, and I'm
the Chief Information Officer for the
Open Compute Project. For those of you
that have not heard about the Open
Compute Project, we're a international
collaborative community focused on
advancing technology in an open way for
the data center industry.
And one of the reasons why we are here
today is because we at the Open Compute
Project have been working to build a
community within Canada to complement
our communities in Europe and in Asia
and across the rest of North America.
So, let's begin. I mean, driven by the
rapid growth of AI, data center design
is undergoing a fundamental shift to
meet new economic and technical
realities. As AI workloads push rack
power levels towards 1 MW, the industry
must rethink how power is delivered,
managed, and coordinated between data
centers, utilities, and the wider
Canadian economy.
And what we want to do here on this uh
discussion and
with our two events is bring together
perspectives from the Open Compute
Project, which tends to dive deep into
technology, along with that from Data
Center Nation, which tends to explore
policy and relationships between the
different uh powers that be within the
economy,
uh and explore how we can collaborate to
support a more integrated and resilient
relationship between data centers and
the Canadian power grid.
So, to kick it all off,
I would like to ask Matt a couple of
questions
uh that really revolve around what are
the challenges and how the different
entities within the Canadian union might
come together. And so, the question I
had wanted to start with is
why are AI data centers representing a
fundamen- fundamentally different power
challenge than traditional cloud
infrastructure?
That's probably the biggest question
that we get asked nowadays, so it's a
great one to begin with.
I mean, from what I've learned speaking
to people in the industry across Canada
and outside of it, AI data centers are
just operating on a completely different
level to what most of are used to with
traditional cloud infrastructure. And
it's not simply more computing, it's
much higher density, significantly more
power per rack. And in some cases,
infrastructure that was never really
designed for this kind of sustained
load. So, the conversation has shifted
pretty quickly from how do we optimize
efficiency to can the power and the
cooling systems even keep up with the
pace demand? And I think that's what
makes this moment feel fundamentally
different from previous waves of data
center growth that we may have seen.
>> [clears throat]
>> You know, and that leads to another
follow-on question. Is the gap that
we're seeing between AI computing demand
for power
and the utility and grid readiness uh to
deliver that and um why do you think
that's becoming such a critical issue at
this juncture?
I think it's such a critical issue at
this juncture because it really all
comes down to the differences in
timelines. So, AI demand is scaling
incredibly fast and companies want
capacity now or they even want to have,
you know, capacity capacity yesterday.
Whereas utilities and grid
infrastructure are operating on much
longer planning and development cycles.
So, for example, I was reading recently
that Canada's planned data center
capacity could be close to 10 times its
current operating base, potentially
growing from 10 or 11 gigawatts today to
well over 100 gigawatts in the near
future. So, when you hear numbers like
that, you do start to understand the
scale of the challenge for utilities
just trying to keep pace.
Because ultimately
every data center project starts with
power. I think that is got to be the new
starting point because without access to
reliable power, you can't even begin
thinking about your servers, your
cooling efficiency, or even AI workloads
at scale. And I think that's where this
growing mismatch between computer design
and energy readiness becomes such a
critical issue.
And you know, Matthew, to follow on with
uh a few numbers
from within the data center arena,
perhaps in 3 4 years ago, when I think
about an enterprise rack, I think about
10 kilowatts, not megawatts, not
gigawatts, kilowatts. And today within
the OCP community and the hyperscale
community, we're now figuring out how
are we going to build 1 MW racks.
That's just one rack and we have to fill
a full data center. So, no surprise on
the numbers you're quoting.
Now, when we think about all of that,
my question is, what's the opportunity
for Canada to position itself as a
global leader in AI infrastructure and
uh luckily clean energy?
I mean, I get from conversation I've
been having with several key players
within the Canadian market, Canada is in
a really exciting and interesting
position right now. So, a huge amount of
the country's IT loads are concentrated
in major hubs like Alberta, Montreal and
Toronto. I think it's around about 90%.
So, there's already a strong
infrastructure foundation there. But,
what people are especially excited about
in Canada is the is their access to
relatively clean energy with a large
percentage coming from a hydro power and
nuclear power. I think it's about 60%
for hydro and 14% for nuclear,
respectively.
Alongside a stable operating and
regulatory environment. And you know,
we're seeing growing interest not only
from the Canadian domestic market, but
also from
the US and other regions like Europe
where organizations are looking for
infrastructure capacity that's both
scalable and sustainable. So, there's a
real opportunity for Canada to position
itself not just as an an [clears throat]
AI infrastructure hub, but as a leader
in how AI growth and clean energy
strategy evolve together.
So, I mean, like what about you, Cliff?
I don't want to do all the talking. I
mean,
what policy, permitting and energy plan
challenges do you see emerging between
governments, utilities and data center
operators?
You know, Matt, it's interesting. The
OCP, we get asked that a lot and uh
you know, our uh
I guess uh comfort zone is really
being hardcore technologists. So, uh the
role we take is a slightly different
angle. It's more about providing the
hardcore data, the technical reality, uh
to the policy makers and letting them
make their decisions. And so, I want to
come at answering this uh question from
a slightly different angle. I would like
to encourage anyone that listens to this
to really understand that it's very
important to stick to the real hardcore
facts about the technology and sadly, I
see so much in misinformation
out there today. In fact, uh
what I see is that uh
the technology challenges
that our
people worry about and that are
impacting permitting and building of
data centers
are actually laden with a lot of
inaccuracies. And it would be great if
we could turn that around and have
people look at the data center industry
in a more positive light rather than
being tried in the court of public
opinion, which is what I see happen now
in some of the worlds
regions of the world and unfortunately,
they make decisions about moratoriums
based on fear, but there's no basis in
reality to some extent for what's going
on. Um
as a Canadian, I personally would not
want this to happen for Canada. So, I'm
hoping that by education and providing
the right information, we can avoid all
of that. And I guess the last thing I
would encourage would be to really
maintain a a positive, constructive,
deal-making attitude between
[clears throat]
all of the above entities, the
governments, the utilities, and the data
center operators. And I think if there's
a collaboration that brings those
parties to the table with the right
information,
then deals will happen and data centers
that are efficient and make sense for
the country will get built.
And so,
let me follow on with a question to you,
Matt, uh that I think is still also is
really very important. Um if we look at
the relationship between data centers
and utilities,
it's clear it needs to evolve from a
transactional model that we have today
to long-term strategic coordination. Uh
the two will go hand in hand and must
succeed together.
Um what what can you add or share about
that?
I'm I'm sure like
me, you've traveled across North America
and Europe and wherever you or I may go,
it's really clear that this traditional
model, uh especially kind of a
transactional, we need power, so give us
power relationship no longer really
works. The scale of AI infrastructure
being planned today means those
decisions carry long-term implications
for regional energy systems, so they
could be affecting homes and schools and
businesses alike.
You know, but there are encouraging
signs. We are seeing earlier engagement
between utilities and data center
operators along with far more
strategic coordination and long-term
planning.
So, if I can give an example, some
hyperscalers are now working directly
with utilities on demand response
programs that allow some data center
loads to flex during periods of peak
grid demand. And in markets where grid
infrastructure
hasn't really kept pace, some operators
are turning to onsite generation, which
really underlines why earlier
coordination matters. So, the
relationship certainly is becoming less
about this one-way transaction and more
more joint planning, thinking together
about how digital infrastructure and
energy systems can evolve side by side.
I mean,
from from also where I'm sitting, aside
from the total power required, why do
you think AI data centers are causing
new challenges for the power grid?
Well,
it means you have to dive a little bit
into the technology to understand what's
happening as we transition from cloud
data centers
to AI data centers. Uh they're very
different workloads.
And uh
you're right. Everyone talks about total
power required, where are we going to
get it?
But for those that are a little more
steeped in the technology and in working
in the power grid, it's not just about
how much power, it's about the
fluctuations that you get hit with.
So, in a traditional cloud data center,
the power demand is fairly stable. 5
gigawatts, 10 gigawatts, 500 megawatts.
Um and it and it doesn't vary that much.
Yes, you add more load, it steps up, but
it stays pretty consistent.
With an AI data center,
uh most people are familiar with GPUs
that are accelerators that do parallel
computation.
Because of the nature of the
computation, you get thousands of GPUs
in sync, all turning on at the same time
and shutting down at the same time.
So, imagine in a world where, let's say
a city like Toronto, all the air
conditioners were synchronized and they
all turned on at the same second.
Clearly, one could appreciate that the
power grid is not designed to handle
that kind of load. Uh we've all seen
blackouts happen in an instant when all
of a sudden too much happens at the same
time.
Well, that's the same thing that goes on
within the data within an AI data
center. and so we need to find ways to
mitigate that partially by coordination
between the grid
and uh the data centers, and also to
look at strategies for efficiencies
within the data center, which is
something that I can tell you the Open
Compute Project community uh is
extremely um
cognizant of and working very hard to
provide solutions. And I didn't mention
it earlier, but within our community, we
have about 200 active projects and over
5,000 engineers that are devoting their
time to help solve some of these
problems.
That's really That's really interesting.
I I mean, as follow, how are How do In
your opinion, how are power delivery
architectures within the data center
changing to support high-density AI
workloads?
Well, there's a total rearchitecture
of the data center being looked at to be
to be frank. So, there's a need for
mitigating and managing the power
fluctuations,
but there's also a need for many
improvements in uh energy use and
efficiency, not only within the IT
equipment, but within the facilities.
As you know, the data center has to take
AC power that from the grid,
but then ultimately computers work on
direct current, and there's a conversion
that needs to be happen. And also the
voltage coming in from the street is
very high, and the direct current
required by circuitry is probably just a
few volts. So, there's a huge
opportunity for efficiencies within the
data center on top of managing
fluctuations, and that's uh part of what
the part of the 200 projects that I
talked to you about uh are focused very
much on that. Now, one of the major
shifts that uh people will be talking
about in the industry is to move to
supply
from this from the data center to the
data hall of 800 volts. And the reason
that's interesting is because it's
mimicking some of the work that's being
done for electric vehicles and copying
some of the technologies that have been
developed for the car charging industry.
This allows for much better power
conversion efficiencies within the data
center to make use of every drop of
power that we can get from the
street to build to power AI clusters.

these higher voltages in the data center
and 800-V DC is safety issues
that we have to look at what are the
ways in which the data center facility
people now need to treat the power
distribution system within the data
center.

about is that um
the other work that's going on is in
coming back to mitigating power
fluctuations
between the AI data center and the grid,
one mechanism that's being explored is
on-site data center-wide energy storage
systems. So, you mentioned on-site
generation, but just as big as on-site
generation is on-site storage, and
therefore people are exploring many
different energy storage systems that uh
can store quite a lot of power and be
that buffer
when all those GPUs turn on, which is
significant change from the architecture
where storage systems in the past were
really about uh backup for when the
power went out, not for being used in
dynamic fashion to help mitigate load
load bursts.

center boundary to allow data centers to
become more integrated with the power
grid?
That's a really good question and a lot
of energy is being spent there,
uh no pun intended,
in terms of the people working on that.

really we have to start to rethink
the facilities and the IT equipment and

you have the data center building

critical, we have to find a way to bring
together the management systems inside
the data hall that are managing power

power from the street. And today, one of
those big problems is that

never any work to bring those two
systems together. They're effectively
working independently. So, that's a new
territory and to help with that, the

a relationship with the Electrical and
Power Institute out of California and it
now we have been now began discussions

collaboration between these two worlds

efforts will be required to support a
more coordinated relationship between
utilities and next generation data
centers?

uh in order to coordinate within the
data center, there're going to be a
number of standardizations

capability to preside prevent a unified
view
to the to the power grid from the data
center utility.

there needs to be a standardization of
how the data center
management systems will communicate and
pass information and share data with the
power grid.

that without looking at the issue of
security.
Just within the data center facility of
itself, imagine if it's a co-location
facility,
typically the ownership of the building
and the supply systems to the data hall

putting their equipment there. So all of
a sudden you have two legal entities
that you need to bridge from security
perspective. And then now we need to go
out to the street and bridge with the
power grid. So there're going to be a
lot of security issues to tackle as

what are the industry collaborations
that will be required over the next 5
years

bottlenecks and really move towards
sustainable growth cuz we all want to
get there. I'd be great Matt to hear
what you think.

question they always ask for their
crystal ball, right? But um, I mean from
where I'm sitting in Canada
particularly, the next 5 years will
require much closer collaboration
between data centers, utilities,
governments, regulators, you know, the
list could go on. It's because the AI
infrastructure is growing faster than
the traditional power and also the
permitting systems were potentially
designed for.

are power availability, but there's
transmission capacity, and there's also
those permitting timelines. And solving
these issues, they're going to require
earlier engagement and much more
long-term planning across the whole
ecosystem.

real advantage. You know, we talked
about the access to low-carbon power,

depend on building digital and energy
infrastructure together, not treating
them as separate conversations that
happen in silos.

industry discussions and chats like this
today are becoming important, and not
just to what you guys do, but also folks
with us at DCM Toronto, which is
happening over in June 26th, and the
focus is increasingly on how the sector
plans to collaborate for that long-term
growth. And of course, you'll be there
as well. You'll be giving a presentation
powering the 1 MW
rack data center. So, we'll be fantastic
to continue this conversation, of
course,
in person.

could data centers evolve from passive
energy consumers into active
participants in grid operations? What
would your answer be?

uh we have to move from thinking of a
data center site as a building
with a connection to the grid and
a data hall.
We have to take the perspective that
it's an ecosystem.

uh generation, and I think there's a big
interest in the next 5 years in our
community to start to look at different
co-generation op- options from wind
farming to solar to small nuclear
reactor, small-scale nuclear reactors.

well. So, those we need to look at that
entire ecosystem when designing a data
center site, which is quite a different
model of thinking, and it's going to
involve yet other communities that
our community is not necessarily engaged
with yet today.
Uh the other thing I want to mention is
that it's going to
take uh getting past certain barriers
people and build collaborative
relationships to move remove those
barriers.
And I want to reinforce that
now, more than ever, is the time to act.
The fact is, we are in the middle of an
AI technology inflection point.
And those that seize the opportunity
with an early market mover advantage
tend to come out the winners. And so, I
am hoping, I believe, that that's what
the leaders of the world will do, and we
will see those pockets of AI emerge
in the world where it needs to do where
it needs to do so.
Uh I wanted to mention
that, in conclusion,
that both OCP and Data Center Nation are
holding events the same week, that is
June
9th in Toronto and 10th and 11th in
Montreal. So, for those of you that are
able to make the journey between the two
cities,
be great. I'll be there with Matt on the
9th, and
then I'll be going on to Montreal on the
10th and 11th.
And on the 9th, I believe we'll be
focusing a bit more on the policy and
the regulatory issues with a little bit
of technology, because Matt, I actually
looked at the schedule, and I noticed
that quite a few of people from OCP
community are actually speaking
at Data Center Nation.
In fact, there's a couple of speakers
that are coming on to Montreal
afterwards and speaking again at our at
OCP Canada Tech Day. And then for those
that would like a little deeper dive in
technology,
come on out to Montreal.
Uh we'd be happy to host you there.
Nice. And make sure you get your air
miles for all this travel as well within
that week. But uh Clint, thanks so much
for your time. Appreciate you speaking
with me today and I will see you in
person in June. Likewise, and I'm
looking forward to it.
Cheers.
